statements.quote: Pre-registrations, surveys, raw data and reproducible R code are available on the Open Science Framework at (https://osf.io/pdjwh/?view_only=d4d76b6c6e9343e99bcc146a68fbd578).
statements.locator: PDF pp. 11-12, Materials and Methods, opening paragraph

statements.quote: As preregistered, we found that participants who used an LLM generated more hypotheses than participants who did not use an LLM but were otherwise unconstrained (e.g., they could use search engines and the Internet).
statements.locator: PDF p. 4, Summary of Findings

statements.quote: Instead, we asked all participants at the end of the study to report the websites they visited during the experiment and, as preregistered, excluded the small number of participants in no-LLM conditions who used LLMs from further analyses (SI Appendix, Table S4).
statements.locator: PDF p. 5, Paradigm, exclusions and SI Table S4

statements.quote: We identified accurate hypotheses based on the playoff betting odds of teams at the time of the experiment, publicly available on the Internet (SI Appendix, Table S1).
statements.locator: PDF p. 5, Paradigm, accuracy benchmark and SI Table S1

statements.quote: Because the primary focus in our paper is the number of hypotheses generated, we did not consistently preregister predictions about confidence or calibration. However, we did explore how LLM use influences accuracy, confidence and calibration, and summarize these findings at the end of the results section (see SI Appendix, Section 3 for details).
statements.locator: PDF p. 5, Paradigm, exploratory outcomes and SI Section 3

statements.quote: As preregistered, compared with participants who did not use an LLM, participants who used an LLM listed more teams (i.e., hypotheses; MLLM = 8.72, SD = 3.76 vs. Mno-LLM = 5.99, SD = 3.56; t(394) = 7.41, p < .001, d = 0.745; Fig. 1).
statements.locator: PDF p. 5, Results, Experiment 1

statements.quote: Once again, in line with our preregistered predictions, participants who used an LLM generated more hypotheses (MLLM = 8.43, SD = 5.31 vs. Mno-LLM = 5.42, SD = 3.39; t(180.4) = 4.94, p < .001, d = 0.676).
statements.locator: PDF p. 5, Results, Experiment 2

statements.quote: These results are consistent with our preregistered prediction that rewarding effort with financial incentives should as effective as using an LLM for increasing the number of hypotheses generated (MLLM, unincentivized = 8.76, SD = 3.77 vs. Mno-LLM, incentivized = 9.22, SD = 4.42; p = .628).
statements.locator: PDF p. 6, Results, Experiment 3

statements.quote: Our participants did not fully appreciate this boost in performance; their percent confidence decreased when they generated hypotheses while using LLMs (Fig.4 and SI Appendix, Table S5).
statements.locator: PDF p. 8, LLMs do not reduce accuracy but do reduce confidence in hypotheses

statements.quote: As preregistered, we excluded a small number of participants in no-LLM conditions who self-reported having used an LLM. Our effects remain robust when including these participants in analyses (see SI Appendix, Section 4).
statements.locator: PDF p. 9, Robustness Checks, Generalization without exclusions

statements.quote: In addition, the effects of using an LLM on number of total and accurate hypotheses generated, percent accuracy, percent confidence, and calibration were robust to comparing participants in the LLM condition separately to those in the no-LLM condition who used a search engine, and to those who did not use a search engine (see SI Appendix, Section 4).
statements.locator: PDF pp. 9-10, Robustness Checks, comparison by search-engine use

statements.quote: Effects of LLM use on number of total and accurate hypotheses generated, actual and estimated hit rates, and calibration remained consistent (all ps < .05) when we control for gender as a covariate in analyses (see SI Appendix, Section 4).
statements.locator: PDF p. 10, Robustness Checks, Generalization across gender

statements.quote: Our accuracy and calibration statistics were based on the betting odds at the time our experiments were conducted. We observe similar results if we use team standings as an alternate accuracy benchmark (see SI Appendix, Section 4).
statements.locator: PDF p. 10, Robustness Checks, betting odds and standings

statements.quote: To evaluate the LLM accuracy, in Experiment 3, participants in the LLM condition copied and pasted the raw output from Perplexity after completing all key dependent measures. Out of 395 participants in the LLM condition, 385 pasted valid entries.
statements.locator: PDF p. 10, LLM output quality and hypothesis generation, availability of raw LLM responses

statements.quote: The average performance of participants who used LLMs corresponded to between the 60th and 81st percentiles of the performance of participants who did not use LLMs (see SI Appendix, Table S12 for details).
statements.locator: PDF p. 11, Benchmarking average performance, SI Table S12

statements.quote: Descriptive analyses show that using LLMs increased hypotheses generated in each quartile across all experiments (see SI Appendix, Tables S13-S16).
statements.locator: PDF p. 11, Benchmarking average performance, SI Tables S13-S16

statements.quote: We coded the total number of unique hypotheses generated by all participants in LLM and non-LLM conditions in each study and found no difference in the number of unique teams listed by the LLM and non- LLM crowds in each study (see SI Appendix, Table S21).
statements.locator: PDF p. 11, Homogeneity of hypotheses generated with and without LLMs, SI Table S21

statements.quote: In an ancillary experiment (SI Appendix, Section 5), participants guessed the (single) occupation of a person after reading a brief profile description. Again, using LLMs increased the number of hypotheses that participants generated.
statements.locator: PDF p. 11, Discussion, ancillary experiment and SI Section 5

statements.quote: Please see SI Appendix, Table S2 for a summary of number of participants preregistered, dropout rates, and final sample sizes obtained across experiments.
statements.locator: PDF p. 12, Materials and Methods, opening paragraph, SI Table S2

statements.quote: See SI Appendix, Table S1 for the dates we collected data and observed the target sport outcome, for each experiment.
statements.locator: PDF p. 12, Materials and Methods, opening paragraph, SI Table S1

statements.quote: 396 participants recruited from Prolific Academic (Mage = 40.30, 39.7% female, 59.1% male) completed the experiment and passed all pre-registered screenings.
statements.locator: PDF p. 12, Materials and Methods, Experiment 1, preregistered screenings

statements.quote: We designed the questions so a basic level of familiarity with MLB was required to pass (e.g., “How many innings constitute a standard MLB game?”; see SI Appendix, Table S3).
statements.locator: PDF p. 12, Materials and Methods, Experiment 1, screening materials

statements.quote: As preregistered, we analyzed data from all participants who (1) correctly answered all knowledge questions, (2) named at least one team to make the playoffs, (3) did not use an LLM unless explicitly instructed to do so (e.g., in the LLM condition).
statements.locator: PDF p. 12, Materials and Methods, Experiment 1, analysis criteria

statements.quote: 213 participants recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk (Mage= 41.90, 33.8% female, 65.3% male) completed the experiment and passed all pre-registered screenings.
statements.locator: PDF p. 13, Materials and Methods, Experiment 2, preregistered screenings

statements.quote: 803 participants recruited from Prolific Academic (Mage= 42.38, 40.3% female, 58.8% male) completed the experiment and passed all pre-registered screenings (as used in Experiment 1). We used the same preregistered exclusion criteria as in Experiment 1.
statements.locator: PDF p. 13, Materials and Methods, Experiment 3, preregistered screenings

statements.quote: 400 participants recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk (𝑀𝑒𝑎𝑛#$%= 40.87, 35.20 female, 64.5% male) completed the experiment and passed all pre-registered screenings (as used in Experiment 2).
statements.locator: PDF p. 13, Materials and Methods, Experiment 4, preregistered screenings

deposits.notes:
The URL is printed in the paper and repeated in both form.data_and_code URLs; recorded once. The OSF API title is AI Hypotheses Generation. Node metadata says public=false, but the paper's published view_only token grants anonymous read access: the page, metadata, file listings and downloaded data all returned HTTP 200 without an account. Thus access is public via the published share link, not publicly indexed.

All 44 files were enumerated in five folders: Data (9), Code (7), Pre-registration (6), Odds and standings files (8), Qualtrics (14). Qualtrics pagination was followed. The children API returned 0, the provider API listed only osfstorage, and the wikis API returned 0. No SI Appendix document was present in these listings. No explicit license was exposed in the node metadata, file listing or inspected code headers; license is null.

The repository currently labels six main experiments plus an ancillary experiment and was modified after the saved manuscript. Mapping was checked using downloaded surveys, raw question labels and code; do not match filenames to saved-study numbers mechanically. {"S1": "Data/data_raw_exp2.csv; Code/code_exp2.R; Qualtrics/Qualtrics_exp2.docx", "S2": "Data/data_raw_exp3.csv; Code/code_exp3.R; Qualtrics/Qualtrics_exp3.docx", "S3": "Data/data_raw_exp6.csv and Data/data_exp6_column_AI-output_url_replaced_with_content.csv; Code/code_exp6.R; Qualtrics/Qualtrics_exp6.docx", "S4": "Data/data_raw_exp4.csv; Code/code_exp4.R; Qualtrics/Qualtrics_exp4.docx", "S5": "Data/data_raw_AS1.csv; Code/code_aexp1.R; Qualtrics/Qualtrics_aexp1.docx"}

rows_checked=803 and columns_checked refer specifically to Data/data_exp6_column_AI-output_url_replaced_with_content.csv (1,413,702 bytes), the processed participant-level file for the saved paper's S3. It contains exactly 803 rows, 99 columns, and 803 distinct nonempty prolificID values. Every row has condition, agent, incentive, hypothesis, unique_hypo_number, accuracy_number and accuracy_perc. The four condition counts are ai_noinc=199, human_noinc=204, ai_inc=202, human_inc=198. The four hypothesis-count means and sample SDs round to the values in the saved PDF p. 6 (8.76/3.77, 6.56/3.47, 9.87/3.34, 9.22/4.42 respectively). AIoutput_adjusted is nonmissing for 395 rows; nonmissing does not establish that every entry is valid LLM output.

has_outcome_scores=true is directly confirmed for the processed S3 file. The other mapped studies provide raw participant responses and R scoring/cleaning code, not precomputed score tables in the inspected CSVs. The primary processed file includes hypothesis_1 through hypothesis_29, standardized team text, accuracy counts/proportions, and standings-based alternatives. All nine CSVs and all seven R files were fetched with HTTP 200 and examined in memory; no downloaded file was saved.

S1: data_raw_exp2.csv has 770 records below the CSV header, including two Qualtrics question-label/import-id records; 768 response records with distinct ResponseId values before exclusions, 69 columns. Arm: condition (ai/human). Texts: hypothesis_1_h_noinc, hypothesis_2_a_noinc.

S2: data_raw_exp3.csv has 304 records including two metadata records; 302 distinct ResponseId records before exclusions, 134 columns. Arm: condition (ai/human). Texts: hypothesis_1_h, hypothesis_1_a. Repeated confidence_MC header names require preserving duplicate-column positions or using the authors' readr name repair.

S3 raw: data_raw_exp6.csv has 1,400 records including two metadata records; 1,398 distinct ResponseId records before exclusions, 82 columns. Arms: agent, incentive, condition. Texts: hypothesis_1_h_noinc, hypothesis_2_a_noinc, hypothesis_3_h_inc, hypothesis_4_a_inc; AIoutput is also present.

S4: data_raw_exp4.csv has 631 records including two metadata records; 629 distinct ResponseId records before exclusions, 261 columns. Arm: condition (human_human, human_ai, ai_human, ai_ai). Texts: hypothesis_1_h-h, hypothesis_2_h-h, hypothesis_1_h-a, hypothesis_2_h-a, hypothesis_1_a-h, hypothesis_2_a-h, hypothesis_1_a-a, hypothesis_2_a-a.

S5 candidate ancillary file: data_raw_AS1.csv has 1,651 records including two metadata records; 1,649 distinct ResponseId records before exclusions, 326 columns. Arm: condition (human_human, human_ai, ai_human, ai_ai); profile identifies the presented profile. Occupation texts are in hypothesis_1_[h-h/a-a/a-h/h-a]_1 through _12 and the corresponding hypothesis_2_ columns. The occupation task is verified in the survey and raw question labels; exact correspondence to the absent historical SI Section 5 is inferred from the matching ancillary task. This is not an analyzed N. Some timing and ChatGPT_check headers repeat.

Additional current-repository experiments, not assigned to studies in this saved form: data_raw_exp1.csv has 570 records and 83 columns; data_exp1_irrelevant_symptom_flagged.csv has 423 records and 64 columns; data_raw_exp5.csv has 1,595 records and 56 columns. These were inspected in memory but not treated as the saved paper's S1 or S5.

Raw counts include screenouts, previews/test responses and incomplete responses as applicable; they are not randomized or analyzed participant counts. No complete participant-flow reconstruction was performed. Data/code must be aligned with the saved manuscript before deriving final study counts.

The R scripts were read, not executed. code_exp4.R and code_exp6.R reference filenames with '(new order)' that are not present verbatim in the listing; code_exp6.R also references 'data exp 3 AI output manually added.csv'. The available raw and processed filenames therefore need to be reconciled before execution. The scoring code explicitly lists accepted team names and computes counts/proportions, but its lists do not by themselves establish the numerical betting-odds threshold.

what_we_could_compute: S1-S4: arm/cell-specific means, sample SDs, SEs and analyzed counts for number of unique hypotheses, number of accurate hypotheses and participant-level accuracy proportions. S3 is directly computable from the 803-row processed file; S1, S2 and S4 require reproducing the posted cleaning and scoring rules on the raw exports.

Open item 4: the raw exports contain assignment, screening, completion and tool-use fields that permit reconstruction of exclusions and analyzed arm counts. Exact randomized totals additionally require verifying that the exports include every randomized participant and removing previews/test records; raw row counts must not be used as randomized N.

Open item 11: recompute unique-team counts by arm and factorial cell, team frequencies and between-participant diversity/overlap, with uncertainty obtained by resampling participants. The original SI Table S21 and its exact uncertainty/pooling method were not found.

Open items 2 and 12: compute S3 results separately with/without incentives and S4 results for each stage-assignment cell or any-stage-AI pooling, and compare those groupings with Figure 4. The current files do not alone prove which historical plotting code generated the saved figure.

Open item 10: reproduce accurate-hypothesis counts and accuracy proportions using the explicit accepted-team lists in the R code, with posted odds/standings source PDFs available. The numerical threshold that originally selected those teams still needs confirmation.

Open item 8: the ancillary occupation-response file can support participant hypothesis counts, arm means/SDs/SEs and occupation-text diversity after applying its cleaning script. Exact alignment with the unavailable saved SI Section 5 and the final analyzed cohort remains to be checked.
notes:
Read all 240 lines of the saved markdown, including references and end-of-document figure legends, and checked the PDF text for statement wording and page locations. The PDF has 17 pages and no embedded files; the SI Appendix cited throughout is not included. Statements are verbatim PDF text with whitespace normalized, preserving source spelling and text-layer glyphs; all occurrences of SI Appendix and preregistration terminology were checked for coverage.

The classification is supported by an actual downloaded and inspected participant-level table with unique participant IDs, experimental assignments, observed outcome scores and hypothesis texts. Confidence is high for public data availability, while historical version correspondence and complete reconstruction of cohorts require further analysis.

Search results: no additional relevant deposit was found. The four DataCite author-search hits were two DOI records for a different online-review replication package (10.5281/zenodo.21873792 and 10.5281/zenodo.21873793) and two thesis records on relevance insensitivity (10.6082/yd4ye-pbh26 and 10.6082/uchicago.2903). Zenodo initially rejected size=100 with HTTP 400 because anonymous requests allow at most 25; both searches were repeated with size=25 and returned 0. OSF's author-name query uses its specified title filter, so it tests author-name mentions in project titles, not a contributor-wide author index; private projects shared by view-only links need not appear.

The SSRN publisher landing page returned HTTP 403 with a bot-check page. No login, account creation, access request, CAPTCHA solving or bypass was attempted. No publisher supplementary-file inventory or newer manuscript could be inspected. The two non-data reference URLs on PDF p. 16 were checked with the hyphens preserved from the PDF, since the markdown loses line-end hyphens. The PDF's OSF hyperlink annotation incorrectly includes trailing ').'; its literal URL returns only an HTML app shell. The correctly delimited link printed in the paper and supplied by the form works with the OSF API.

One data repository and four linked preregistration records are listed as deposits; the latter contain materials only. No independent participant dataset was found by the repository searches. No SI Appendix was found among OSF's 44 files. Open items about the abstract total discrepancy, overlap across papers and the creativity-scope/codebook decisions are not settled by this availability check.

All network requests used python urllib with User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1 and no login or identifying email. Data and materials were held in memory; only the requested JSON was written.
